headline: Saudi cold chain heads for 785,000 pallet positions as pharma raises the standard
deck: Temperature-controlled throughput is modelled to rise from 13.6 million tonnes to 17.2 million by 2031, and the hardest cargo is the smallest.
excerpt: Cold chain is one of the declared segments at the Saudi Warehousing & Logistics Expo. Refrigerated warehouse capacity in the Kingdom is projected at around 785,000 pallet positions by 2031, and pharmaceutical requirements are pulling the technical standard up faster than food volumes are pulling capacity.
content:
Cold chain sits among the declared segments at the Saudi Warehousing & Logistics Expo, and it is the part of the logistics market where the engineering content is highest and the tolerance for failure lowest.

The volumes are moving. Temperature-controlled throughput in the Kingdom is modelled to reach around 17.2 million tonnes by 2031, against 13.6 million tonnes in 2025, with refrigerated warehouse capacity projected at approximately 785,000 pallet positions. The market itself is put at roughly $2.17bn in 2026, growing at a mid single-digit rate through the end of the decade.

A pallet position is a more honest unit than square metres for this sector, because a refrigerated warehouse is a volume rather than an area. Height is usable, racking is dense, and the cost that matters is the cost of holding a cubic metre at a temperature, which is set by insulation, air management, door discipline and refrigeration plant efficiency rather than by land.

The engineering divides sharply by temperature band. Ambient chilled produce at two to eight degrees is a well-understood problem with mature equipment. Frozen at minus eighteen is harder and more energy-intensive but equally well established. The difficult category is pharmaceutical, and it is difficult for reasons that are regulatory as much as thermal: the requirement is not only to hold a temperature but to prove continuously that it was held, across every transfer, with an auditable record and validated equipment.

That requirement is what is currently pulling the Saudi market upward. The Saudi Food and Drug Authority's programme for breakthrough medicines has driven investment into specialised infrastructure, reported at more than $581m, and operators have been building to the standard rather than retrofitting to it. NAQEL Express committed SAR 200m to a multi-temperature facility in Jeddah dedicated to biologics and vaccines — a category where a single excursion outside the permitted band writes off the consignment.

The climatic context makes all of this harder than the equivalent operation in Europe. Ambient temperatures for much of the year mean that every dock door opening, every trailer standing on a yard, and every gap in a handover is a thermal event. The engineering answers are known — dock shelters, air curtains, staged loading, refrigerated cross-dock — and they cost money that a warehouse designed for dry goods does not spend.

The energy question follows directly. Refrigeration is the dominant load in a cold store, and it runs against the same grid whose peak is already set by cooling. Efficiency measures in this sector are not primarily an environmental argument; they are an operating cost argument with an environmental consequence attached, and they are why the refrigeration plant on show at an exhibition of this kind attracts a technical audience.

The Kingdom's 59 planned logistics zones and dual-coast access improve the redundancy position for temperature-controlled goods, which matters more for pharmaceuticals than for food: a single route failure on a validated cold chain is a compliance event, not merely a delay.

The expo runs from 8 to 10 September at the Riyadh International Convention & Exhibition Center.
author: Jakson Gudawela
